analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give construction workers a paid 15-minute break every four hours.
analysis.headline: A bill guaranteeing construction workers one paid 15-minute break for every four hours worked was introduced with 14 House Democrats behind it, but the House committee it went to never acted on it and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to require construction employers to give workers at least one paid 15-minute rest break for every four hours of work. It would ban employers from retaliating against workers who take a break or complain to the Labor Department, require written notice of these rights in the worker's primary language at hiring, and require bilingual signs at construction sites. It died in the House Education and Labor Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers — the people who erect, remodel, repair, and demolish buildings — would get a guaranteed paid 15-minute break every four hours, an anti-retaliation shield, and notice of these rights in their own language at hiring. The bill defines the right broadly, covering workers hired as contractors as well as direct employees, and it explicitly does not override state laws, local ordinances, or union contracts that already require longer breaks. Workers who are retaliated against could win reinstatement, back pay, and equal liquidated damages through the Department of Labor.

how_it_helps.text: Construction workers would receive at least one 15-minute paid rest break for every four hours of work — roughly two paid breaks per standard 8-hour day — on top of any meal periods.

The bill prohibits employers from retaliating against or discriminating against workers who request or take breaks, or who file a complaint with the Department of Labor, and lets a worker who is retaliated against recover lost wages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, reinstatement, or promotion.

At hiring, employers must explain these rights in the worker's primary language, and work sites must post signs in English and Spanish — a meaningful protection in a workforce with many Spanish-speaking laborers.

The definition of 'construction employee' reaches workers hired as contractors of an employer, not just direct employees, and the bill explicitly does not weaken any federal, state, or local law or union contract that requires longer breaks.
If an employer violates the break requirement and fails to fix it within 30 days of notice, the Labor Secretary may assess an administrative penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Construction employers — general contractors and the firms that employ or hire construction labor — would pay for roughly 30 minutes of paid break time per 8-hour shift per worker, plus the cost of written notices and required bilingual site signage, and they would face penalties and liquidated-damages liability for violations. To the extent those costs are passed on, some of the expense could flow into project costs.

drawbacks.text: The mandate falls on construction employers, including small contractors who operate on thin margins, who would absorb roughly 30 minutes of paid time per worker per 8-hour day and the administrative cost of notices, bilingual signage, and recordkeeping.
Enforcement depends on workers filing complaints with the Department of Labor; a worker who fears losing a job may never file, and the bill does not create a proactive inspection program.
The bill is narrow: it covers only general construction services and sets a low floor — one 15-minute break per four hours — while leaving actual break frequency and scheduling to the employer.
The Labor Department must first issue regulations on the design and content of the required site signs before employers can fully comply, adding a lag between enactment and effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete but modest: a guaranteed half hour of paid rest across a full construction shift, with real teeth against retaliation. The cost is real but small and predictable — about 30 minutes of paid time per worker per day plus compliance paperwork. The main weakness is not the design but the enforcement model, which relies on individual complaints in an industry where job insecurity makes complaining risky, and the bill's limited scope leaves non-construction workers uncovered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Sylvia Garcia of Texas introduced the bill on July 20, 2022, joined by 10 original cosponsors, including Reps. Porter, Thompson of California, McCollum, Garcia of Illinois, Newman, Norton, Espaillat, Veasey, Green of Texas, and Doggett.
Thirteen House Democrats total signed on as cosponsors, all from the same party.
The bill's only action beyond introduction was referral to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced.
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and no vote ever took place before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction employers are better off because the bill died: they avoid the new paid-break mandate, anti-retaliation liability, and bilingual notice requirements without ever having to cast a vote against it.

for.name: Sylvia Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to guarantee construction workers paid rest breaks and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 13 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 13 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no referral to the floor — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan split can only be read from sponsorship: the sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on, but the committee that buried the bill was also chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would require these employers to provide about 30 minutes of paid break time per worker per 8-hour day, post bilingual notice signs, and face penalties, back pay, and liquidated damages for violations. Their financial interest ran against the workers' guaranteed rest, and the bill never advanced to a vote.

industries.industry: Staffing and labor subcontractors in construction
industries.note: Because the bill defines covered workers to include people hired as contractors of an employer, firms that supply construction labor could not sidestep the mandate by using contract arrangements.
